overall_summary: Analysis of 47 unique Shorts reveals an unmistakable performance divide: extreme planetary astrophysics and second-person immersive survival scenarios ('What If You Fell Into...') consistently generate peak viewership (800–1,050+ views) and highest like-to-view ratios (~3.5–3.8%). Conversely, repeated re-uploads of generic psychology ('Fake memories', 'Songs stuck in head') and overdone space trivia ('Space is silent') collapse below 10–50 views due to audience fatigue and lack of visceral curiosity.

winning_patterns.pattern: Second-Person Extreme Planetary Survival ('What If You Fell Into...')
winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet' (1,029 views, 38 likes), 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice' (972 views, 18 likes), and 'What If You Fell Into the Darkest Planet' (823 views, 15 likes) heavily outpace all other formats.
winning_patterns.action: Standardize the immersive, sensory-rich 'What If You Fell...' framing for extreme cosmic phenomena, maintaining a tight 20–21 second runtime.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles detailing extreme planetary environments like 'TrES-2b Darker Than Coal' (1,030 views, 36 likes) and 'Venus Day Longer Than Its Year' (981 views, 21 likes) drive strong algorithmic engagement without relying on recycled tropes.
winning_patterns.action: Spotlight lesser-known astronomical anomalies featuring sensory extremes (temperatures, gravity, radiation) that challenge baseline intuition.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' was reposted three times, collapsing from 53 views to 10 and 5 views; 'Songs Stuck In Your Head' stalled at 17–71 views.
weak_patterns.action: Retire low-stakes cognitive trivia and eliminate duplicate concept uploads entirely.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Why Space Is Completely Silent' posted multiple times delivered only 34–220 views with minimal engagement.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid standard middle-school science facts; replace passive explanations with visceral high-stakes consequences.

next_video.hook_style: Second-person visceral catastrophe ('What If You Fell...')
next_video.concept: Falling onto a Magnetar (SGR 1806-20), the universe's most magnetic star.
next_video.opening_direction: Instant high-stakes question: 'If you fell toward a magnetar, you would be dead thousands of miles before touching the surface.'
next_video.twist_direction: The magnetic field is so intense it literally stretches your atomic nuclei into needles, turning your bio-chemistry into dissolving static in a millisecond.
next_video.reason: Leverages the proven >1,000-view 'What If You Fell...' structure while moving away from previously covered exoplanets (TrES-2b, Gliese 436b, 55 Cancri e, WASP series) into terrifying compact stellar objects.
fresh_topic_constraints: Do not mention diamond rain, burning ice, coal planets, or molten iron.
Focus strictly on magnetars and magnetic atomic distortion.
Never present speculative physics as mundane fact; emphasize real astrophysics.

experiment: Test whether compact dead stars (magnetars/neutron stars) using second-person survival framing surpass the exoplanet benchmark in both view velocity and comment debate within 48 hours.
